title: Transformers
description: The attention mechanism and architecture underlying modern CV, NLP, and LLMs.
blurb: The attention mechanism and architecture underlying modern CV, NLP, and LLMs.
careerApplications: This is the single most valuable architecture to understand deeply for any AI/ML role today — it underlies virtually every state-of-the-art model in language, vision, and beyond.

lessons.title: Why transformers were created
objectives: Explain the core limitation of recurrent models that transformers solved
Explain how recurrence changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect recurrence with sequential bottleneck and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Before transformers, sequence models (RNNs/LSTMs) processed tokens one at a time, in order — token 100 couldn't be computed until token 99 was done. This made training slow (no parallelism across the sequence) and made it hard to connect distant tokens (information had to pass through every step in between, degrading over long distances).
examples:
# RNN: token_100 depends on token_99 depends on token_98 ... -- inherently sequential, slow to train
# Transformer: every token can attend directly to every other token, all at once -- parallelizable
commonMistakes: Assuming transformers are just 'a bigger RNN' — the architectural shift (parallel attention vs sequential recurrence) is the actual innovation, not just scale.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is one of the most common 'explain why transformers matter' interview questions in AI/ML roles.

lessons.title: Tokens, embeddings & positional encoding
objectives: Explain why transformers need explicit positional information
Explain how token embeddings changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect token embeddings with positional encoding and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Text is tokenized (as in the NLP track) and each token is converted to an embedding vector. But since a transformer looks at all tokens simultaneously rather than in sequence, it has no inherent sense of ORDER — 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' would look identical without help.
examples:
token_embedding = embed(token)          # what the token IS
position_embedding = position_encode(i)  # where the token IS in the sequence
final_input = token_embedding + position_embedding
commonMistakes: Assuming attention alone preserves word order — it doesn't; positional encoding is a deliberately added mechanism to inject that information back in.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding this addition is a common follow-up question after explaining self-attention.

lessons.title: Queries, keys & values
objectives: Explain the query/key/value framework attention is built on
Explain how query changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect query with value and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Every token produces three vectors: a Query (what am I looking for), a Key (what do I contain, for others to match against), and a Value (what I actually offer if selected). Attention compares each token's Query against every other token's Key to decide how much focus to put on each, then combines their Values weighted by that focus.
examples:
# conceptually, for one token's query:
# score_i = query . key_i   (how well this key matches what I'm looking for)
# attention_weights = softmax(scores)   (turn scores into a 0-1 distribution)
# output = sum(attention_weights_i * value_i)   (blend of others' values, weighted by relevance)
commonMistakes: Trying to memorize Q/K/V as arbitrary labels instead of the underlying intuition (searching for X, offering to be matched on Y, giving Z if picked) — the intuition is what actually helps you.
lessons.careerRelevance: Transformer engineers use this when debugging attention shapes, reading model implementations, optimizing inference, and understanding why attention behaves the way it does.

lessons.title: Self-attention & multi-head attention
objectives: Explain what self-attention computes and why multiple heads are used
Explain how self-attention changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect self-attention with context-aware representations and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Self-attention lets every token look at every other token in the SAME sequence to build a context-aware representation — 'bank' next to 'river' vs 'bank' next to 'money' end up with different representations because attention lets context flow in.
examples:
# self-attention: EVERY token attends to every other token in its own sequence
# multi-head: run this 8 (or more) times in parallel with different learned weights,
# then concatenate the results -- each head can specialize in a different pattern
commonMistakes: Assuming one attention head captures everything relevant — different heads reliably specialize in different relationship types, which is exactly why using several matters.
lessons.careerRelevance: This is directly used when implementing, profiling, debugging, or serving transformer models and when reasoning about long-context cost.

lessons.title: Encoder/decoder structure & masking
objectives: Contrast encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder transformers, and explain masking
Explain how encoder-only changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect encoder-only with decoder-only and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An encoder builds a rich representation of an entire input (good for understanding tasks, e.g. classification).
examples:
# masked self-attention during generation:
# when predicting token 5, the model can attend to tokens 1-4,
# but token 5's attention scores to tokens 6+ are masked to -infinity
# (so softmax gives them ~0 weight -- can't see the future)
commonMistakes: Confusing masking (which prevents seeing future tokens during generation) with padding (which just marks unused positions in a batch) — they solve different problems and use different mask.
lessons.careerRelevance: Knowing whether a given model is encoder-only, decoder-only, or both is basic, expected vocabulary in any LLM-adjacent role.

lessons.title: Training objectives & fine-tuning
objectives: Explain how transformers are pretrained and then adapted to specific tasks
Explain how pretraining changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect pretraining with next-token prediction and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Most transformers are pretrained on a huge, generic objective — for GPT-style models, simply 'predict the next token' on massive text corpora, which turns out to teach a remarkable amount of general language ability.
examples:
# pretraining objective (simplified): given 'The cat sat on the', predict 'mat'
# -- done over a MASSIVE, generic corpus
# fine-tuning: given a small dataset of (support ticket -> correct category) pairs,
# adapt the pretrained model to this specific classification task
commonMistakes: Assuming fine-tuning is always necessary — for many tasks today, prompting a strong pretrained model (see the Prompt Engineering track) gets you most of the way without any fine-tuning at.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding the pretrain-then-adapt paradigm is the conceptual foundation the entire LLM track builds on directly.

lessons.title: Inference, context windows & computational limits
objectives: Explain what a context window is and why attention is computationally expensive
Explain how context window changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect context window with quadratic attention cost and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: The context window is the maximum number of tokens a transformer can consider at once — anything beyond it is simply invisible to the model.
examples:
# attention cost scales as O(n^2) in sequence length n
# double the context window -> roughly 4x the attention compute
# this is why '1 million token context' is a genuinely hard engineering achievement, not just a bigger number
commonMistakes: Assuming you can just keep feeding a model more and more context 'for free' — cost and latency scale non-linearly, and very long contexts can also dilute the model's effective attention over.
lessons.careerRelevance: Context-window trade-offs are a practical, daily concern in RAG and AI-agent system design, covered directly in those tracks next.

lessons.title: Self-attention: a worked example
objectives: Compute a tiny self-attention pass by hand
Explain how worked example changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect worked example with softmax and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Working through a small, concrete attention calculation makes the mechanism tangible. Given query, key, and value vectors for a few tokens, computing the dot-product scores, applying softmax to get attention weights, then taking a weighted sum of values shows exactly how a token's representation gets updated using context from every other token.
examples:
# tiny worked example (2 tokens, 2-dim vectors):
# query for 'bank' = [1, 0], keys = [[1,0], [0,1]] for 'bank' and 'river'
# scores = dot products = [1, 0]
# softmax([1,0]) approx [0.73, 0.27] -- 'bank' attends mostly to itself here
# output = 0.73*value_bank + 0.27*value_river
commonMistakes: Trying to reason about attention only abstractly without ever computing a concrete example -- the mechanism is much clearer once you've traced actual numbers through it.
lessons.careerRelevance: Being able to walk through this calculation is a common, concrete interview exercise for roles touching transformer internals.

lessons.title: Transformers beyond text: vision & multimodal models
objectives: Explain how the transformer architecture extends beyond text
Explain how vision transformer changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect vision transformer with ViT and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Vision transformers (ViT) apply the same self-attention mechanism to images, by splitting an image into patches and treating each patch like a token. Multimodal models combine text and image (or audio) understanding in one architecture, often using cross-attention so text tokens can attend to image patches and vice versa.
examples:
# Vision Transformer (ViT) intuition:
# split a 224x224 image into 16x16 patches -> 196 'tokens'
# feed these patch embeddings through the SAME kind of transformer
# encoder used for text -- attention works the same way, just on patches
commonMistakes: Assuming transformers only work for text -- the same core self-attention mechanism generalizes to images, audio, and combinations of modalities.
lessons.careerRelevance: Vision transformers and multimodal architectures are now common in production computer vision and generative AI systems.

exercises.title: Why not just use an RNN
exercises.prompt: Explain in 2-3 sentences why an RNN can't process a sequence in parallel the way a transformer can.

exercises.title: Positional encoding necessity
exercises.prompt: Explain what would go wrong if you fed a transformer token embeddings with NO positional information at all.

exercises.title: Compute a tiny attention score
exercises.prompt: Given query [1,0], and two keys [1,0] and [0,1], compute the dot-product attention scores against each key and say which token gets more attention.

exercises.title: Encoder, decoder, or both
exercises.prompt: For 3 tasks (sentiment classification, text generation, machine translation), say whether an encoder-only, decoder-only, or encoder-decoder model fits best.

exercises.title: Diagnose a masking bug
exercises.prompt: A text-generation model's outputs look suspiciously perfect on the training set but garbage at real generation time. Causal masking was implemented incorrectly -- what's the likely bug?
exercises.hint: mask isn't applied, so training let the model 'see' future tokens it can't see at real generation time

exercises.title: Context-window cost scenario
exercises.prompt: Doubling a model's context window roughly quadruples attention compute. Explain why, and what this implies for very-long-document use cases.

exercises.title: Explain parallelization's benefit
exercises.prompt: Why can transformers train faster on modern hardware than RNNs, which process tokens one at a time?
exercises.hint: transformers process all tokens in parallel, unlike RNNs' inherently sequential processing

exercises.title: Identify encoder vs decoder use
exercises.prompt: For a translation task (input sentence to output sentence), would an encoder-decoder or a decoder-only architecture fit more naturally? Why.
exercises.hint: encoder-decoder -- naturally separates understanding the input from generating the output

exercises.title: Reason about context window limits
exercises.prompt: A user's conversation exceeds the model's context window. What happens to the earliest messages, and why does this matter?
exercises.hint: earliest messages get truncated/dropped -- the model can no longer 'see' them, which can lose important earlier context

quiz.q: The main architectural innovation transformers introduced over RNNs is:
options: bigger models
parallel attention instead of sequential recurrence
using GPUs
removing embeddings

quiz.q: Positional encoding exists because:
options: attention has no inherent sense of token order
tokens are too large otherwise
it speeds up training
it replaces embeddings entirely

quiz.q: Causal (masked) attention during generation prevents:
options: using GPUs
the model attending to future tokens it hasn't generated yet
using multiple attention heads
tokenization errors

quiz.q: Self-attention's computational cost scales with sequence length as roughly:
options: constant
linear
quadratic
logarithmic

quiz.q: Fine-tuning is used to:
options: replace pretraining entirely from scratch every time
adapt a pretrained model to a specific task with less data
increase the context window
remove positional encoding

quiz.q: Why were transformers created, largely in response to what limitation?
options: they weren't responding to any limitation
RNNs' sequential bottleneck, which prevented parallelization and struggled with long-range dependencies
transformers came before RNNs existed
to reduce model size only

quiz.q: What does 'sequential bottleneck' refer to in older architectures like RNNs?
options: a memory limitation only
having to process tokens one at a time in order, preventing parallelization across the sequence
a synonym for overfitting
a hardware requirement

quiz.q: Why does parallelization matter for training large models?
options: parallelization has no real benefit
it lets modern hardware (GPUs/TPUs) process much more data simultaneously, dramatically speeding up training
parallelization only helps with inference, not training
parallelization always reduces model accuracy

quiz.q: What is a token embedding?
options: a literal picture of a word
a dense numeric vector representation of a token, capturing learned meaning
a synonym for positional encoding
a type of loss function

quiz.q: What problem does positional encoding solve?
options: it solves a memory limitation
self-attention alone has no inherent sense of token order, so positional encoding injects that order information
positional encoding removes the need for embeddings
it only matters for very short sequences

quiz.q: Why is self-attention naturally 'order-agnostic' without positional encoding?
options: it isn't order-agnostic, order is automatic
attention computes relationships between all token pairs based on content, with no built-in notion of sequence position
order-agnostic means it ignores all tokens
this only applies to the first token

quiz.q: What are queries, keys, and values in attention?
options: three separate unrelated models
three learned projections of each token used to compute how much each token should attend to every other token
a synonym for encoder, decoder, and embedding
types of loss functions

quiz.q: What does dot-product attention compute?
options: a random score for each token
a similarity score between a query and each key, used to weight how much attention to pay to each value
the model's total parameter count
the token's position only

quiz.q: What does self-attention let each token do?
options: only look at itself
incorporate context from every other token in the sequence, weighted by relevance
only look at the previous token, like an RNN
ignore all other tokens entirely

quiz.q: What does multi-head attention provide over single-head attention?
options: no real benefit, it's just slower
multiple parallel attention computations, letting the model attend to different kinds of relationships simultaneously
multi-head attention removes the need for embeddings
it only works for very long sequences

quiz.q: What does 'context-aware representation' mean, produced by self-attention?
options: a token's meaning is fixed regardless of context
a token's representation is updated based on the specific other tokens surrounding it in that sequence
context-awareness only applies to the first token
it means the model ignores context entirely

quiz.q: What characterizes an encoder-only architecture?
options: it only generates new text, never understands input
it processes and understands input text, commonly used for tasks like classification
it has no attention mechanism
it requires no training data

quiz.q: What characterizes a decoder-only architecture?
options: it can only read text, never generate it
it generates text one token at a time, commonly used for tasks like open-ended text generation
decoder-only models have no self-attention
it requires two separate input sequences

quiz.q: What is an encoder-decoder architecture typically used for?
options: only classification
tasks that transform one sequence into another, like translation, where encoding and generation are naturally separate stages
tasks with no input text at all
only image tasks

quiz.q: What does causal masking enforce in a decoder?
options: nothing, masking is cosmetic
that a token can only attend to earlier tokens, not future ones, preserving the left-to-right generation order
masking removes the need for attention
masking only applies to the first token

quiz.q: What is pretraining, for a large language model?
options: fine-tuning on a specific narrow task
initial large-scale training on broad text data, often using next-token prediction, before any task-specific adaptation
a synonym for inference
deleting the model's weights

quiz.q: What does next-token prediction train a model to do?
options: classify images
predict the most likely next token given the preceding context, the core pretraining objective for many LLMs
translate between languages only
detect objects in images

quiz.q: What does fine-tuning a pretrained transformer typically involve?
options: training an entirely new model from random weights
further training the pretrained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset to specialize its behavior
deleting the pretrained weights first
only changing the tokenizer

quiz.q: What is parameter-efficient fine-tuning?
options: retraining every single parameter from scratch
techniques that adapt a pretrained model to a new task while updating only a small subset of parameters, saving compute
a synonym for pretraining
removing all parameters before training

quiz.q: What is a context window?
options: the model's total training dataset size
the maximum amount of text (in tokens) a model can consider at once when generating a response
a type of attention head
the model's file size on disk

quiz.q: Why does quadratic attention cost matter for long sequences?
options: it doesn't matter, cost is constant
self-attention's compute cost grows roughly with the square of sequence length, making very long sequences expensive to process
quadratic cost only affects training, never inference
cost decreases as sequences get longer

quiz.q: What happens when a conversation exceeds a model's context window?
options: nothing, all context is always retained
earlier content gets truncated or dropped, since the model can no longer 'see' it
the model automatically summarizes everything perfectly
the context window expands automatically

quiz.q: Why is inference compute a practical concern for deploying large transformer models?
options: inference is always free/instant
generating each token requires real computation, and this cost scales with model size and sequence length, affecting cost and latency
inference compute only matters during training
larger models always run faster

quiz.q: What does a Vision Transformer (ViT) treat as 'tokens'?
options: individual pixels only
patches of the image, similar to how words are tokens for text
entire images as one single token
color channels

quiz.q: What does cross-attention enable in a multimodal model?
options: nothing useful
text tokens can attend to image patches (or vice versa), letting the model relate information across different modalities
cross-attention only works within a single modality
it replaces the need for embeddings entirely
